Welcome toStarlight through Dust

Starlight crosses a dust cloud to a telescope: what arrives, and how far away does the star seem?

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

About: interstellar extinction and reddening, and what they do to a distance from the distance modulus

About this simulation

On screen
Top: a Sun-like G2 V star on the left sends blue (445 nm), yellow (551 nm) and red (650 nm) dots of light along a beam to a telescope on the right. They cross in about 3 s through an oval dust cloud whose grains are drawn in proportion to the optical depth. Dots taken out of the beam fly off sideways inside the cloud. The beam's width follows its flux, and its colour follows the light it carries. Below: the line of sight on a logarithmic distance axis from 50 to 20 000 pc. It shows the star at its true distance, a ghost where the astronomer places it when ignoring the dust, and a ghost where the colour-excess correction places it.
Controls
AV sets the cloud's extinction in the V band, 0 to 3 mag. d sets the true distance of the star, 100 to 3000 pc. ℛV sets the dust's ratio of total to selective extinction, 3.1 to 5. Changing any of them restarts the stream of light.
Measured
mV = ℳV + 5 log10(d/10 pc) + AV with ℳV = 4.83. mB − mV = 0.65 + EB−V, with EB−V = AV/ℛV. The uncorrected distance puts all of mV − ℳV down to distance. The corrected distance first removes 3.1 × EB−V, because the astronomer always assumes ℛV = 3.1. The two distance rows, and the two ghosts, appear once the card that asks about them has been answered.
Assumptions
All the dust is in one foreground cloud. Its extinction Aλ is taken to fall linearly with 1/λ between the B and V bands, fixed by AV and EB−V = AV/ℛV; real extinction curves are close to this in the optical. The dust itself is assumed not to glow at these wavelengths, and the star's intrinsic colour is taken as known from its spectral class.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Adding dust

Set the extinction to AV = 0, the distance to d = 1000 pc and the ratio to ℛV = 3.1. Before raising the extinction to AV = 1, predict what happens to the light that reaches the telescope.

2 · The uncorrected distance

Keep AV = 1, d = 1000 pc and ℛV = 3.1. The astronomer knows the absolute magnitude of the star from its spectral class and ignores the dust. Before looking at the line of sight below the scene, predict the uncorrected distance.

3 · A more distant star

Keep AV = 1 and ℛV = 3.1, and before moving the distance slider from 1000 pc to 3000 pc, predict the ratio of the uncorrected distance to the true one.

4 · Twice the extinction

Set the distance back to d = 1000 pc, keep ℛV = 3.1, and before raising the extinction from AV = 1 to AV = 2, predict the new ratio of the uncorrected distance to the true one.

5 · Correcting with colour

Set the extinction back to AV = 1, keep d = 1000 pc and ℛV = 3.1. The astronomer measures the colour excess EB−V, about 0.32, and multiplies it by 3.1 to estimate the extinction. Before looking at the corrected ghost, predict where it lies.

6 · Dust of a different kind

Keep AV = 1 and d = 1000 pc, and before raising the ratio of the dust from ℛV = 3.1 to ℛV = 5, as in a dense cloud, predict what happens. The astronomer still assumes 3.1.

7 · Summary

Dust dims starlight and reddens it: blue light is removed more strongly than red, so mV grows by AV and the colour index by EB−V = AV/ℛV.

Ignored, the extinction makes a star seem farther by the factor 10AV/5, whatever its distance.

The colour excess, the observed colour minus the colour the spectral class predicts, measures the dust: AV ≈ 3.1 EB−V for ordinary dust. Where the dust has a different ℛV, the corrected distance is off.

Starlight through a Dust Cloud

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

This sim sends light from a star through a dust cloud to a telescope. You set how much dust there is, how far away the star is and what kind of dust it is, and the sim shows the light that arrives and the distance an astronomer would work out from it.

What you'll learn

  • How the dust changes the light that reaches the telescope.
  • How the colour of the light measures the dust.
  • How the distance worked out from the light depends on the dust.
The set-up: starlight crosses the cloud on its way to the telescope.

What's on screen

  • Dots in blue, yellow and red: light at 445, 551 and 650 nm crossing the beam and the dashed cloud. Dots the dust removes scatter out of the beam.
  • Strip below: the line of sight on a logarithmic distance axis, with the star as a dot and dashed circles for where the astronomer places it.
  • Readouts: mV, mB − mV and EB−V, and two distances.
See itLook at the set-up with no dust. Watch for: a clear beam of mixed blue, yellow and red dots, a star at 1000 pc on the strip, and AV = 0.00 mag.

03

Dust makes the star fainter and redder

The grains in the cloud scatter and absorb starlight out of the beam, and they remove short wavelengths more strongly than long ones (notes, Fig. 81). The flux that arrives is Fλ = Fλ,0 e−τλ (6.1), where τλ is the optical depth of the dust. In magnitudes the dimming is the extinction Aλ:

Aλ = −2.5 log10(Fλ/Fλ,0) = 2.5 τλ log10 e ≈ 1.086 τλ
Equation (6.2). One magnitude of extinction is an optical depth of about one.

At AV = 1 mag, mV rises from 14.83 to 15.83 and only 40% of the V light gets through. Because AB is larger than AV, blue loses more: 30% gets through at 445 nm and 48% at 650 nm, for the sim's ℛV = 3.1. The star is fainter, and redder.

The fraction of the light that gets through at AV = 1 mag, ℛV = 3.1.
See itRaise the extinction from 0 to 1 mag, at d = 1000 pc and ℛV = 3.1 (all three are set for you). Watch for: the dots thinning and the beam turning from white to orange, with mV reading 15.83 mag and mB − mV reading 0.973 mag.
04

The colour excess measures the dust

A star's spectral class fixes its intrinsic colour (mB − mV)0, 0.65 for this star. The colour excess is how far the observed colour sits above it (notes, 6.4):

EB−V = (mB − mV) − (mB − mV)0 = AB − AV

The colour excess can be measured without knowing the distance; the extinction cannot. The two are tied by the ratio of total to selective extinction (6.5), which is about 3.1 along most lines of sight through the diffuse medium and up to about 5 through dense clouds:

ℛV = AV / EB−V
So EB−V = AV/ℛV. At AV = 1 mag, EB−V = 0.323 for ℛV = 3.1 and 0.200 for ℛV = 5.
Colour excess against extinction. The same dimming reddens less when ℛV is larger.
See itAt AV = 1 mag and d = 1000 pc, raise ℛV from 3.1 to 5. Watch for: mV staying at 15.83 mag while EB−V falls from 0.323 to 0.200 mag.
05

Ignoring the dust puts the star too far away

The distance modulus gains the extinction (notes, 6.3), where ℳV is the absolute magnitude of the star:

mV − ℳV = 5 log10(d / 10 pc) + AV

An astronomer who knows ℳV from the spectral class, but ignores the dust, puts all of mV − ℳV into the distance. The distance comes out too large by the factor 10AV/5.

For AV = 1 mag the factor is 100.2 = 1.585, so a star at 1000 pc is placed at 1585 pc, about 60% too far. One magnitude is a factor 2.512 in flux, but the distance goes as the square root of the flux ratio, so it grows only by 1.585.

Key idea. The dimming from dust is read as extra distance, and the star looks 585 pc farther away at AV = 1 mag.
See itRaise the extinction from 0 to 1 mag, at d = 1000 pc and ℛV = 3.1. Watch for: the dashed circle for the dust-ignoring distance moving out along the strip from the star, and Ignoring the dust reading 1585 pc.
06

The same cloud stretches every distance by the same factor

The cloud adds a fixed number of magnitudes, whatever the star's distance, and 10AV/5 does not contain d. At AV = 1 mag a star at 3000 pc is placed at 4755 pc. The error grows from 585 pc to 1755 pc, but the ratio stays 1.585.

The same stretch at two distances, equal in length on a logarithmic axis.

Magnitudes add, so the factors multiply. At AV = 2 mag the factor is 100.4 = 2.512 = 1.5852, and a star at 1000 pc is placed at 2512 pc. It is not twice the AV = 1 factor.

See itAt AV = 1 mag, move the star from 1000 pc out to 3000 pc. Watch for: the dashed circle keeping its distance from the star on the log axis, and Ignoring the dust reading 4755 pc.
See itAt d = 1000 pc, raise the extinction from 1 to 2 mag. Watch for: Ignoring the dust moving from 1585 pc to 2512 pc, not to 3170 pc.
07

The colour excess puts the distance back

The astronomer cannot read AV directly, but can measure EB−V. With an assumed ℛV the extinction is AV = ℛV EB−V, and solving the distance modulus for d gives (notes, 6.6):

d = 10 pc × 10(mV − ℳV − ℛV EB−V)/5
The sim always uses ℛV = 3.1 here.

If the dust really has ℛV = 3.1, then 3.1 EB−V is exactly AV: at AV = 1 mag the corrected distance is the true 1000 pc. If the dust has ℛV = 5, the same dimming comes with only EB−V = 0.200, so the correction removes 0.62 mag instead of 1, and the star lands at 1191 pc, still too far. The notes add that the method needs ℛV to be the same along the path as where it was measured.

Where each distance puts a star whose true distance is 1000 pc, at AV = 1 mag.
AV d ℛV

These sliders move the sim too. The numbers come from the sim's own functions.

See itRaise the extinction from 0 to 1 mag, at d = 1000 pc and ℛV = 3.1, and use the colour excess. Watch for: the violet dashed circle sitting on the star, and Corrected, ℛV = 3.1 reading 1000 pc.
See itNow make the dust denser: raise ℛV from 3.1 to 5. Watch for: the corrected distance moving off the star to 1191 pc, while Ignoring the dust stays at 1585 pc.
08

Where it matters

  • Trumpler, 1930. The distances of open clusters from the magnitudes of their stars came out larger than those from their angular diameters, increasingly so with distance, and the stars were redder than their classes implied. Dust explained both (notes, 6.1).
  • The Galactic plane. Near the Sun the extinction averages about one magnitude for every kiloparsec, though it is very patchy. On average, one kiloparsec of path would make an uncorrected distance too large by about 60%.
  • The Galactic centre. About 30 magnitudes of extinction hide it at visible wavelengths, but the extinction is much smaller in the infrared, where individual stars close to the central source can be seen (notes, §6.1).
09

Summary

In one line. Dust along the line of sight changes the light that reaches the telescope, and the sim follows what that does to a distance worked out from the light.
  • Dust dims and reddens starlight: mV rises by AV and EB−V = AV/ℛV.
  • Ignoring AV makes the distance too large by 10AV/5, the same factor at every distance.
  • The correction with ℛV = 3.1 is exact only for dust with ℛV = 3.1.

Common mix-ups

  • "Dust only moves the star farther away, so its colour is unchanged." The colour index rises from 0.650 to 0.973 at AV = 1 mag.
  • "One magnitude of dust means 2.5 times the distance." 2.5 is the flux factor. The distance factor is its square root, 1.585.
  • "A farther star suffers a bigger factor from the same cloud." The factor is still 1.585 at 3000 pc.

Things to try on your own

  • Set AV = 0 and read both distances and mB − mV.
  • Find the extinction that makes the ignored-dust distance twice the true one: AV = 1.5 mag.
  • At AV = 2 mag and d = 1000 pc, compare the corrected distance for ℛV = 3.1 and 5.
